items.followUp: What is the difference between a saturated and an unsaturated solution?

rubric.why: Checks the defining feature of a dilute solution.
rubric.description: States that a dilute solution contains a relatively small amount of solute.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the relatively small amount of solute in a dilute solution.

rubric.why: Checks the defining feature of a concentrated solution.
rubric.description: States that a concentrated solution contains a relatively large amount of solute.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the relatively large amount of solute in a concentrated solution.

modelAnswer: A dilute solution contains a relatively small amount of solute dissolved in a given amount of solvent.
A concentrated solution contains a relatively large amount of solute dissolved in a given amount of solvent.

items.followUp: How does hydrogen react with oxygen? Write the balanced chemical equation.

rubric.why: Checks the balanced equation for the reaction.
rubric.description: Writes the balanced equation for hydrogen reacting with chlorine.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl.

rubric.why: Checks the reaction condition and product.
rubric.description: Identifies hydrogen chloride as the product and states that the reaction takes place in light.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming hydrogen chloride and mentioning light or sunlight.

modelAnswer: Hydrogen reacts with chlorine in sunlight to form hydrogen chloride.
H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2HCl(g)
The reaction is vigorous and may be explosive in bright sunlight.

items.followUp: Write the equation for the reaction of methane with bromine in diffused sunlight.

rubric.why: Checks the products formed in methane chlorination.
rubric.description: Identifies chloromethane and hydrogen chloride as the products.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving CH₃Cl and HCl as the products.

rubric.why: Checks the balanced substitution equation and its condition.
rubric.description: Writes the balanced equation and specifies diffused sunlight.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl in diffused sunlight.

modelAnswer: In diffused sunlight, one hydrogen atom of methane is substituted by a chlorine atom.
CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl

items.followUp: State two limitations of Rutherford’s atomic model and one feature of Bohr’s model that addressed them.

rubric.why: Checks the difference in the permitted electron orbits.
rubric.description: Contrasts Rutherford’s unrestricted orbits with Bohr’s fixed permitted orbits.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that Rutherford allowed orbits of any radius whereas Bohr proposed fixed permitted orbits.

rubric.why: Checks the difference in electron energy levels.
rubric.description: Contrasts Rutherford’s lack of definite electron energies with Bohr’s definite energies for permitted orbits.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying this difference in energy levels.

rubric.why: Checks the difference in energy radiation during orbital motion.
rubric.description: States that Rutherford’s revolving electrons radiate energy, whereas Bohr’s electrons do not radiate energy in stationary orbits.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this contrast in radiation.

rubric.why: Checks how the models account for atomic stability.
rubric.description: States that Rutherford’s model could not explain atomic stability, while Bohr’s model accounts for a stable atom.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for contrasting the models’ explanations of stability.

rubric.why: Checks how the models account for atomic line spectra.
rubric.description: States that Rutherford’s model could not explain line spectra, while Bohr explained them through transitions between energy levels.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for contrasting their explanations of atomic spectra.

modelAnswer: Rutherford’s model allowed electrons to revolve in orbits of any radius, whereas Bohr proposed fixed permitted orbits.
Rutherford’s model did not assign definite energies to electron orbits, whereas each Bohr orbit has a definite energy.
In Rutherford’s model revolving electrons radiate energy; in Bohr’s model electrons do not radiate energy in stationary orbits.
Rutherford’s model could not explain atomic stability, whereas Bohr’s model describes a stable atom.
Rutherford’s model could not explain line spectra, whereas Bohr explained them by transitions between energy levels.

items.followUp: Define an ionic bond and explain how it forms, giving one example.

accept: share one or more pairs of electrons
sharing one or more pairs of electrons
rubric.why: Assesses the definition of a covalent bond.
rubric.description: Defines a covalent bond as a bond formed when atoms share one or more pairs of electrons.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for a clear definition involving sharing electron pair(s) between atoms.

rubric.why: Assesses the single covalent bond and an example.
rubric.description: States that a single covalent bond has one shared pair of electrons and gives a valid example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the explanation and an example such as H₂ or Cl₂.

rubric.why: Assesses the double covalent bond and an example.
rubric.description: States that a double covalent bond has two shared pairs of electrons and gives an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the explanation and an example such as O₂.

rubric.why: Assesses the triple covalent bond and an example.
rubric.description: States that a triple covalent bond has three shared pairs of electrons and gives an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the explanation and an example such as N₂.

modelAnswer: A covalent bond is formed when two atoms share one or more pairs of electrons.
A single covalent bond has one shared pair of electrons; for example, H—H in H₂.
A double covalent bond has two shared pairs of electrons; for example, O=O in O₂.
A triple covalent bond has three shared pairs of electrons; for example, N≡N in N₂.

items.followUp: Define boiling point and state two factors that affect it.

rubric.why: Checks the meaning of vapour pressure.
rubric.description: Defines vapour pressure as the pressure exerted by a vapour in equilibrium with its liquid in a closed container.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the equilibrium vapour-pressure definition.

rubric.why: Checks the effect of temperature on vapour pressure.
rubric.description: States that vapour pressure depends on temperature and increases as temperature rises.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming temperature and giving its effect.

rubric.why: Checks dependence on the identity of the liquid.
rubric.description: States that vapour pressure depends on the nature of the liquid.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming the nature or kind of liquid.

rubric.why: Checks the effect of intermolecular attraction.
rubric.description: Explains that stronger intermolecular forces result in a lower vapour pressure.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking stronger intermolecular forces with lower vapour pressure.

modelAnswer: Vapour pressure is the pressure exerted by a vapour in equilibrium with its liquid in a closed container.
Vapour pressure depends on temperature; it increases when temperature increases.
It depends on the nature of the liquid.
Stronger intermolecular forces hold molecules in the liquid more strongly and result in a lower vapour pressure.
